audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages (p.96 penultimate root stress; p.98 Main Stress rule (70) and Secondary stress rule (72)) are verbatim on the rendered page scan of the NUSA 33 scan we hold, at the stated pages. The secondary-stress rule and examples (71) match the catalog rule string exactly (initial secondary only when at least one syllable separates it from the penultimate primary). (2) Deciding source is a dedicated 47-pp phonology article (1991) by long-term SIL fieldworkers; Glottolog 5.1 lists no reference grammar or later phonology for Coastal Konjo, and the one modern theoretical paper with Konjo data (Basri, Broselow & Finer, held under sela1260) restates penultimate primary stress and clitic extrametricality, silent on secondary stress. OLAC 429; SIL 403); list of works to obtain is limited to Friberg 1995 CAD

sources.citation: Basri, Hasan, Ellen Broselow & Daniel Finer. 'The End of the Word in Makassar Languages.' Author manuscript from D. Finer's Stony Brook publications page (later published, to my unverified recollection, in Borowsky et al. (eds.) 2012, Prosody Matters: Essays in Honor of Elisabeth Selkirk, Equinox).
sources.quote: 'Stress in all three languages normally falls on the penultimate syllable, regardless of syllable makeup ... Stress may be analyzed as the realization of a bisyllabic trochaic foot aligned with the right edge of the PWd ... true suffixes fall inside the stress domain while phrasal clitics fall outside it'; monomorphemic antepenultimate stress only with a final epenthetic vowel. No statement on secondary stress.
